transcript: In the late 1970s, Exxon - yes, the  oil company - declared war on IBM. It is strange. But since the start of the decade,   the company had been slowly  buying technology startups. Including one very iconic chip company. Then in 1978, they declared their  intention to merge those startups   together and take on Big Blue. Did Exxon succeed? In this video, we look at that time  when the most iconic oil company in   modern history took on the  office equipment business. ## Beginnings In 1911, the US government ordered John  Rockefeller’s Standard Oil trust to be broken up. Since 1899, all the trust's corporate  subsidiaries were kept under a single   holding company called Standard Oil of New  Jersey. Which I shall call here, Jersey Standard. The way the breakup specifically worked  was that Jersey Standard was ordered to   distribute all of the shares in  its subsidiaries to its existing   shareholders. Such shares were worth about  half of the firm's net value of $600 million. It was done kind of like a dividend. Famously,   the shares of the various subsidiaries tripled  or quadrupled in the years after the spinoff,   skyrocketing Old Man Rockefeller's net worth  afterwards. Maybe he should have done it earlier! Since the dissolution was cut along pre-existing  corporate structures, they did not birth a bunch   of integrated companies. Rather, the 34 or  so subsidiaries were carved up by activity   or geographical region. Some had refining, others  crude, some just pipelines. Nobody had everything. Eight of the larger siblings split the  old Standard Oil trademark. Since the   siblings for some reason felt that bearing  the name of a ruthless monopoly had value,   they used it within their  own operating geographies. However, it also gave the public  the impression that the Standard   Oil beast still lived. Which may  or may not have been the case. In 1923, Jersey Standard managed  to trademark the name "Esso",   which is the phonetic rendition of S.O., or  "Standard Oil". And by the 1930s, this name would   become widely used - much to the annoyance  of siblings like Standard Oil of Indiana. Esso became an iconic name in its own right.  But I will continue to refer to the company as   Jersey Standard. It seems to be what they  called themselves throughout this time. Until of course 1972, when the company finally  realized that its association with the Standard   Oil name was detrimental to its reputation  and future growth, and underwent a massive   rebranding to Exxon. The new name unified  a patchwork quilt of regional trademarks. ## Jersey Now, Jersey Standard was the heart of the  Standard Oil Goliath, but it was not some   empty shell corporation. It was an actual  operating company with productive assets. This included - among other things - major  refineries in the US east and Louisiana   plus allocated marketing/distribution  networks in parts of the US East Coast. The company also kept all of the old  Standard Oil's foreign interests,   including Imperial Oil in Canada. Later in 1947, Imperial strikes  oil at Leduc No. 1 in Alberta,   turning Canada into the  oil giant that it is today. So Jersey was by itself almost a fully  integrated giant, except for the small,   little, teeny-weeny thing of not  having any crude oil production. Initially, they can get crude  from their Standard Oil siblings,   but with those siblings slowly vertically  integrating and barging into each other's   territory - remember that whole Esso thing  - future competition seemed inevitable. So in 1919, Jersey Standard bought 50% of  the fast-growing Texas oil producing firm,   Humble Oil Refining. And abroad,   the company secured oil production interests  in Latin America, Venezuela in particular. After World War II - which by the way got Jersey  nearly tarred and feathered by the US public   thanks to an alleged 1929 under-the-table  deal with the IG Farben horror machine in   Germany to delay US production of synthetic  rubber - Jersey entered the Middle East. In late 1946, they bought into the Aramco  Company - the core oil company in Saudi   Arabia and today the fifth largest company in the  world by revenue. By 1948, they would own 30%. Then in 1954, they joined the  multinational consortium that   took over operations of Iran's  oil industry after the brief   nationalization and embargo that eventually  led to the removal of Iran's prime minister. ## Oil Glut So as you can see, Jersey Standard  is an oil company's oil company. The largest oil firm in the world, with $7.5  billion of revenues in 1958. Second on the Fortune   500 after General Motors. Executing complicated  projects in every continent around the world. So what got them started down the path  to selling office equipment? Well,   like as with many a tale of strange and ultimately  embarrassing antics, this one begins in the 1960s. While the Iranian consortium agreement stabilized  the oil markets, it - plus the rise of the Soviet   oil production from the Volga-Urals - deepened  an oil glut. In 1958, Jersey Standard sold more   oil than ever, yet profits were just a third  of what they were at the start of the decade. Forbes Magazine argued that a revolution  had taken place in the world economics   of oil and Jersey Standard had to adjust.  If it only kept on doing nothing but oil,   Jersey will struggle to  make money for shareholders. In 1960, Jersey Standard's CEO Monroe  "Jack" Rathbone requested an evaluation   of the company's investment philosophy. The  board responded by setting up a commission   led by finance executive David J.  Jones to write a detailed report. The Jones Report laid out Jersey  Standard's investment policy but   also evaluated the oil industry in  the decade ahead. It concluded that   the circumstances behind the oil  glut were expected to continue. The Report wasn't wrong about that,   by the way. Posted oil prices remained  stuck at around $2-3 per barrel until 1970. Anyway, the Report's most striking argument  was that oil and gas wasn't a growth business   anymore. That didn't mean it was time  to leave oil and gas behind - though it   did suggest that the company exercise  more prudence in its oil investments. It meant that future opportunities in oil  and gas will show ever-worsening returns.   So if Jersey Standard wanted  to become a growth stock again,   then new revenue lines were  needed: Diversification. ## Chemicals The Jones Report convinced the board that some  diversification was necessary, but into what? The most obvious direction was to expand in  chemicals. Jersey Standard had already been   making certain petrochemicals through  an "Esso Chemical" brand for 40+ years.   Stuff like rubbing alcohol, acetone, or  feedstocks like ethylene and propylene. But those were basic chemicals. And the business  line was pretty small - just $250 million of   revenue in 1959. It was essentially an  afterthought. But if the oil feedstock   is going to stay so cheap, then why not go  and produce higher value products with it? So the board agreed to aggressively push into  various plastics and chemical fertilizers through   an official new Esso Chemical subsidiary  company with its own set of executives. Jersey then drastically raised  Esso Chemical's annual investment   budget - which had averaged a modest $53  million from 1961 to 1963 - to $257 million   in 1964. Its executives moved quickly  to spend that money all over the world. The fertilizer push was particularly  bold - motivated by the United Nations'   contemporaneous call to raise food  production and abolish world hunger. Plants were ordered in Central America,  the Caribbean, the Philippines, Malaysia,   Pakistan, Lebanon, Greece, Spain,  the Netherlands, and Canada. Jersey Standard’s internal research institute  Esso Research was funded with 10% of corporate   profits - and allocated a quarter of  that budget for petrochemicals: Exploring   opportunities in steel-making, agriculture  (like with mulch), and building materials. An interesting product of this time  was fluidized iron ore reduction,   a method to turn fine iron ore into metallized  iron by reacting it with hot reducing gas.   The result is Directly Reduced Iron (DRI)  which can be put into an electric arc   furnace to make steel - thus skipping the  traditional sintering and pig iron steps. ## 2 Fast 2 Furious Anyway. The general problem  with chemical diversification   is that the other oilmen know about it too. Other oil giants like Phillips, Royal  Dutch Shell, Standard of Indiana,   and Standard of California (now Chevron)  were already doing petrochemicals.   This was a tough space and they are  not going to just let Jersey waltz in. Rathbone acknowledged this  competition, telling Forbes: > "Petrochemicals have become fashionable to  enter. Everybody and his brother, for example,   seems to be making polyethylene. But this dashing  into chemicals is going to lose a lot of money for   some companies, because petrochemicals are not  a guaranteed gold mine ... And it won't be us." Famous last words. The chemicals effort  moved with a speed that irritated Jersey's   top management. As early as late October 1963,  Rathbone complained about being asked to approve   new fertilizer and plastic plants in Cyprus  and Colombia that he had never heard of before. By 1965, it had become clear  that things had gone too fast,   too furious. Esso Chemical returned just 4%  on its net total assets. Once-hyped spaces   like thermoplastics and fertilizers were  oversupplied and losing millions of dollars. In late 1966, Jersey's top management decided  to curtail the chemical program and refocus on   profits. The US chemicals division made  money, but the foreign undertakings and   joint ventures were a mess. It would  take several years to clean it all up. In the 1970s, Esso Chemical performed far  better by focusing on specialty chemicals   that might not deliver eye-popping top line  numbers, but do well on the bottom line. By   the end of the decade, they were turning out  hundreds of millions of dollars of profits. ## Jersey Enterprises In 1963, Jersey Standard founded a  new entity called Jersey Enterprises   to explore "new investments"  and further diversification. As part of this effort, Jersey Enterprises  chose ten large categories that can possibly   birth a new $100 million company. They  looked both inside and out for candidates. One of their first projects  was to build a test factory   for Esso Research's aforementioned  fluidized iron ore reduction method.   They spearheaded the build in the  town of Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. In January 1964, Enterprises  acquired American Cryogenics   Inc for $37 million. The idea was to  acquire technology to make industrial   gas. Unfortunately the technology wasn't  competitive and they were dropped in 1968. Another potentially delectable venture was a 1965  partnership with Nestle's affiliate in Guatemala   to develop a protein food called WO-100 - made  from harvested bacteria raised up on hydrocarbons. The resulting "food" if you can call  it that was a bland white powder.   Young chicks fed it were reported to  have performed "poorly" unless they   were also given extra vitamins. I don't  think this food ever made it to market. Another technology that did not work out was  the concept of using petroleum residues to bind   soil and aggregates together into building  blocks for housing. But it cost as much as   making cement blocks, and they couldn't  prove it can hold together for as long. Efforts in medical instruments, nuclear energy and  fuel cells fell by the wayside as well. Slowly,   Jersey Enterprises' original ten  fields got winnowed down to just   a few. One of those was information technology. ## Vydec Jersey’s first IT success was Vydec,  the maker of a word processor. Dedicated word processor devices  emerged in the early 1970s. They   were typewriters with a video screen  and data storage attached to them.   Such systems let people write and edit stuff  without printing it all out onto paper. According to Ben Sykes, who ran  Jersey Enterprises at this time,   Vydec first approached them in 1971. The  company began as a computer terminal project   at Hewlett-Packard run by Patrick  P. DeCavaignac and two other people. But when HP decided to terminate the project,   DeCavaignac thought it had potential. So HP  gave permission to start a company with it.   Working out of a basement, the team put  together a word processor with a video   screen and floppy drive. One of the first  such word processors to have a floppy. After several VC firms passed, they found  Jersey Enterprises through a "friend of a   friend". Jersey studied the firm for what  seems today like a rather long time before   agreeing in early 1973 to invest $500,000  (about $3.7 million today) for 40% equity.   They would eventually come to own over 80%. Thanks to Daddy Exxon - remember they changed   their name in 1972 - Vydec was able  to fund the manufacturing of these   word processors plus bootstrap a large  sales team to sell them to customers. The space was pretty competitive  - you had guys like Linolex,   Lexitron, AES, IBM, and of course,  my personal favorite Wang Labs. But   Vydec held its ground and grew fast - opening  over 50 sales offices across the country. In 1977, they made an estimated $24  million in revenue, which today would be   $147 million - quite the sum for many companies. But Exxon that year made $48.6  billion unadjusted from the oil   business. $24 million compared to that is peanuts. This is a running theme with all of  Exxon Enterprises' little projects.   How does any of it compare to oil? When  asked about the long term plan in 1976,   Exxon managers said that there was no  "grand scheme or master plan" but it   did seem like they wanted to get a few $100  million companies together in the portfolio. The investment portfolio would soon grow  to include a hodge hodge of companies like   Periphonics Corporation, which made a  computer that imitated human voices. And Micro-Bit, which was developing a type of  memory called electron beam accessed memory.   You can certainly see how it all fit together! ## Zilog By far, Exxon Enterprises' most famous investment  was the iconic microprocessor company, Zilog. The company that would become Zilog  was founded by several ex-Intel people   including Federico Faggin, the  wunderkind designer of Intel's   first commercial microprocessor  4004 as well as the 8008 and 8080. In an oral history for the  Computer History Museum,   Faggin recalled that after leaving Intel,  he and his cofounder Ralph Ungermann told   a reporter about their intention to  form a new microprocessor company. The resulting published article  in Microprocessor Digest caught   the attention of Exxon Enterprises.  Exxon’s people reached out and said   that they would be in the area in  a few days and wanted to meet up. That got Faggin and Ungermann moving on  drawing up a business plan - which involved   a single chip microprocessor called  the 2001. When the Exxon team arrived,   they hit it off pretty well and in 1975, Exxon  agreed to fund them as the sole investor. After this, the company consistently  advertised itself as an Exxon affiliate. That 2001 chip didn’t work out but  they got something better. In mid-1976,   they launched the Zilog Z80, the iconic 8-bit  microprocessor that challenged the Intel 8080. Many enthusiasts fondly remember  the Z80 to this day. It is a good   chip. I think articles about it still  rank on HackerNews from time to time. ## Exxon and Zilog At first the relationship between  Zilog and Exxon went very well. Faggin has acknowledged that Zilog  probably would have never gotten   off the ground without Exxon. Competing  in the semiconductor industry - even if   you do not immediately intend to build a  fab - means shelling out a lot of money. After a devastating stock  bubble in the early 1970s,   the VC funding market dried up. Faggin  recalled just $10 million of technology   investments being made in all of 1975.  Exxon Enterprises was the sole game in town. And in the early days, cofounder Ungermann noted  that the Exxon name helped nab many a design win.   He remembered telling customers that they had  "the money of Exxon and the brains of Intel".   That Exxon money did fund their fab after the  Z80’s success, so it definitely helped them. But as time went on, the relationship changed.  Exxon's resources became a double-edged sword.   Former employee Bernard Pueto  later said that the oil giant   gave them too much money and too many directions. It got Zilog into things they shouldn't have done,   and their young managers didn't have the  experience to know when to push back. Before long, Faggin was spending more time  over in New York with Exxon trying to keep   them out of the way than he was in California  working with the customers. Disagreements   over Exxon led to Faggin and Ungermann's own  relationship fraying - and the latter exited. ## Taking on IBM Perhaps the most impactful thing  was that Exxon - unbeknownst to   Zilog - was planning to compete with IBM. Exxon's tentative first steps into  the office equipment space began in   1975 when it initiated development of  a new typewriter. After several years,   they had themselves the Qyx  "intelligent" typewriter. Powered by a Z80 chip, this $1,390 typewriter was  billed as the first to be electronic - built with   70% fewer moving parts. The idea was that you  can connect it to the Vydec word processor. Another product followed - an early version of the  fax machine called the QWIP. It allowed users to   send pages of text or images to others in a few  minutes. Yes, that is what a fax machine does. These new products apparently gave Exxon  Enterprises confidence and they called   their companies' various senior executives to  come to their New York HQ to brainstorm the   future of IT ... and formulate a grand  strategy to take down IBM and Xerox. In late 1978, Exxon announced that it had  consolidated the three major products - Vydec,   QWIP, and Qyx - along with 12 other prior Exxon  investments to create Exxon Information Systems. Exxon wanted EIS - which Sykes said turned $100  million in 1978 and $200 million in revenue in   1979 - to become a big player in the office  equipment space within three to five years. Some analysts believed that Exxon's  characteristic discipline and focus   can help it win. One at a firm  called Yankee Group said in 1980: > "It seems likely that the [office system]  business they are building now will rival,   if not surpass, their oil business ultimately" Yankee Group forecasted that the whole  IT market would be worth $150 to $200   billion by the end of the 1980s and  that Exxon could capture 10% of that. More than a few were not so positive. Several  cited the size argument again. Exxon pumped $84   billion of revenue in 1979 - fired up by the  high oil prices of the second energy crisis. Even if EIS got as big as - let's say Xerox,  which sounds like a fantastic feat - that adds   only $7 billion in revenue. For Exxon,  that's a drop of oil into the barrel. Yet others pointed that smashing  together a bunch of small,   unrelated companies and expecting success is  a fool's errand. Exxon Information Systems   began life with 6,000 employees and  an organization chart 40 pages long. John Cunningham, EVP at Wang  Labs, colorfully put it: > "If God himself came down in a junior  businessman's uniform, worked very hard for   three years, and got very lucky, he'd still have  a tough time pulling those companies together" ## Withdrawal It did not take long for Exxon Information  Systems to start proving Cunningham right. Exxon had the "luck" of buying into  a suite of old-time word processors   and office products on the eve of  the PC revolution. In April 1977,   Apple introduced the Apple II microcomputer.  Cheap and aesthetically pleasing,   it did wonders when combined with the  powerful Visicalc spreadsheet program. The growth of digital microcomputers like  the Apple II - including ironically the   TRS-80 computer powered by Zilog's own  Z80 - quickly ate into the antiquated   office equipment market that Exxon was pursuing. And unfortunately, Exxon had neither  the corporate structure nor culture   to handle a fast moving, talent-centric  environment like information technology.   Faggin recalled just how slowly  the company made decisions, saying: > So anytime there was a decision to be made, the  lower guy on the totem pole would look up, the   other guy would look up at the next, and Ben Sykes  who was the senior guy would say, “Yes,” or “No.” The company struggled to develop new products. The  second-generation Qwip machine took six years to   develop and came to the market dead-on-arrival.  Literally. The paper feeder jammed. There were other product problems.  Vydec was locked out of US government   work due to security issues. A Qyx  intelligent typewriter intelligently   caught on fire inside Exxon’s  own New York City headquarters. And people at Exxon's marketing division  in Houston explicitly preferred Wang.   They were eventually forced to take Exxon  equipment but returned them a year later. IBM wasn't exactly the dancing elephant either.  But they had the advantages of a titanic sales   force, cutting edge technology, and the  cultural perception of "nobody got fired   for buying IBM". Even with all that, they still  needed a rebel to go forth and make the IBM PC. Exxon's status as a competitor by the way  guaranteed that IBM would not choose the Zilog   Z80 to power the PC. Of course, that was not  the only reason behind the decision - it never   is just one - but Faggin later confirmed it did  matter in IBM picking the Intel 8088 over the Z80. Ben Sykes told the press  that he expected EIS to turn   $400 million in 1980 and keep doubling  to hit a billion within a few years. But   when Exxon increased its investment, its  previously torrid revenue growth stalled. In 1981, Exxon twice cut its workforce down  from 6,000 employees to just 4,000. They   would shut down some of the QWIP fax machine  factories and reorganize the whole division. The IBM PC came out that year and changed  the world - further obviating Exxon   Information Systems' already antiquated  lineup. Yet Exxon staggered on for two   more years - its annual report chirping about  losses narrowing and new products coming out. Then in 1984, the company finally  admitted what everyone else could see:   That this was not working. They started selling  off business lines to whoever was interested. Everything else was closed down.  According to a former manager,   hundreds of leftover obsolete QWIP machines  were taken to a dump and bulldozed. ## Conclusion In the end, Zilog was the last company  inside the Exxon Enterprises portfolio to go. They were sold off in the late 1980s as  a management buyout backed by the private   equity firm Warburg Pincus. The buyout price  was very cheap at about 4 times free cash flow. Warburg would take it public in 1991  before another acquisition in 1997 for   $527 million - earning the PE firm 12 times  return on a small $17 million investment. Several of Exxon's other diversification  ventures did better than the office fiasco.   They made good money from developing  residential and commercial real estate   in and around Houston via the  firm Friendswood Development. They saw more mixed results with minerals  - funding and pursuing various coal, zinc,   molybdenum, and copper mines around the world. And   of course we earlier talked  about the Chemicals business. But the experience of Exxon Information  Systems imprinted itself deeply upon   Exxon's senior managers. In 1993,  Lee Raymond became Exxon's CEO   and intensified the core message:  They were oil men. Nothing more. Over the next two decades, he redoubles the  company's efforts in oil and gas. By the late   2000s, ExxonMobil had become the biggest, most  profitable company the world had then ever seen.

the end of the decade, they were turning out  hundreds of millions of dollars of profits.
## Jersey Enterprises
In 1963, Jersey Standard founded a  new entity called Jersey Enterprises
to explore "new investments"  and further diversification.
As part of this effort, Jersey Enterprises  chose ten large categories that can possibly
birth a new $100 million company. They  looked both inside and out for candidates.
One of their first projects  was to build a test factory
for Esso Research's aforementioned  fluidized iron ore reduction method.
They spearheaded the build in the  town of Dartmouth, Nova Scotia.
In January 1964, Enterprises  acquired American Cryogenics
Inc for $37 million. The idea was to  acquire technology to make industrial
gas. Unfortunately the technology wasn't  competitive and they were dropped in 1968.
Another potentially delectable venture was a 1965  partnership with Nestle's affiliate in Guatemala
to develop a protein food called WO-100 - made  from harvested bacteria raised up on hydrocarbons.
The resulting "food" if you can call  it that was a bland white powder.
Young chicks fed it were reported to  have performed "poorly" unless they
were also given extra vitamins. I don't  think this food ever made it to market.
Another technology that did not work out was  the concept of using petroleum residues to bind
soil and aggregates together into building  blocks for housing. But it cost as much as
making cement blocks, and they couldn't  prove it can hold together for as long.
Efforts in medical instruments, nuclear energy and  fuel cells fell by the wayside as well. Slowly,
Jersey Enterprises' original ten  fields got winnowed down to just
a few. One of those was information technology.
## Vydec
Jersey’s first IT success was Vydec,  the maker of a word processor.
Dedicated word processor devices  emerged in the early 1970s. They
were typewriters with a video screen  and data storage attached to them.
Such systems let people write and edit stuff  without printing it all out onto paper.
According to Ben Sykes, who ran  Jersey Enterprises at this time,
Vydec first approached them in 1971. The  company began as a computer terminal project
at Hewlett-Packard run by Patrick  P. DeCavaignac and two other people.
But when HP decided to terminate the project,
DeCavaignac thought it had potential. So HP  gave permission to start a company with it.
Working out of a basement, the team put  together a word processor with a video
screen and floppy drive. One of the first  such word processors to have a floppy.
After several VC firms passed, they found  Jersey Enterprises through a "friend of a
friend". Jersey studied the firm for what  seems today like a rather long time before
agreeing in early 1973 to invest $500,000  (about $3.7 million today) for 40% equity.
They would eventually come to own over 80%.
Thanks to Daddy Exxon - remember they changed
their name in 1972 - Vydec was able  to fund the manufacturing of these
word processors plus bootstrap a large  sales team to sell them to customers.
The space was pretty competitive  - you had guys like Linolex,
Lexitron, AES, IBM, and of course,  my personal favorite Wang Labs. But
Vydec held its ground and grew fast - opening  over 50 sales offices across the country.
In 1977, they made an estimated $24  million in revenue, which today would be
$147 million - quite the sum for many companies.
But Exxon that year made $48.6  billion unadjusted from the oil
business. $24 million compared to that is peanuts.
This is a running theme with all of  Exxon Enterprises' little projects.
How does any of it compare to oil? When  asked about the long term plan in 1976,
Exxon managers said that there was no  "grand scheme or master plan" but it
did seem like they wanted to get a few $100  million companies together in the portfolio.
The investment portfolio would soon grow  to include a hodge hodge of companies like
Periphonics Corporation, which made a  computer that imitated human voices.
And Micro-Bit, which was developing a type of  memory called electron beam accessed memory.
You can certainly see how it all fit together!
## Zilog
By far, Exxon Enterprises' most famous investment  was the iconic microprocessor company, Zilog.
The company that would become Zilog  was founded by several ex-Intel people
including Federico Faggin, the  wunderkind designer of Intel's
first commercial microprocessor  4004 as well as the 8008 and 8080.
In an oral history for the  Computer History Museum,
Faggin recalled that after leaving Intel,  he and his cofounder Ralph Ungermann told
a reporter about their intention to  form a new microprocessor company.
The resulting published article  in Microprocessor Digest caught
the attention of Exxon Enterprises.  Exxon’s people reached out and said
that they would be in the area in  a few days and wanted to meet up.
That got Faggin and Ungermann moving on  drawing up a business plan - which involved
a single chip microprocessor called  the 2001. When the Exxon team arrived,
they hit it off pretty well and in 1975, Exxon  agreed to fund them as the sole investor.
After this, the company consistently  advertised itself as an Exxon affiliate.
That 2001 chip didn’t work out but  they got something better. In mid-1976,
they launched the Zilog Z80, the iconic 8-bit  microprocessor that challenged the Intel 8080.
Many enthusiasts fondly remember  the Z80 to this day. It is a good
chip. I think articles about it still  rank on HackerNews from time to time.
## Exxon and Zilog
At first the relationship between  Zilog and Exxon went very well.
Faggin has acknowledged that Zilog  probably would have never gotten
off the ground without Exxon. Competing  in the semiconductor industry - even if
you do not immediately intend to build a  fab - means shelling out a lot of money.
After a devastating stock  bubble in the early 1970s,
the VC funding market dried up. Faggin  recalled just $10 million of technology
investments being made in all of 1975.  Exxon Enterprises was the sole game in town.
And in the early days, cofounder Ungermann noted  that the Exxon name helped nab many a design win.
He remembered telling customers that they had  "the money of Exxon and the brains of Intel".
That Exxon money did fund their fab after the  Z80’s success, so it definitely helped them.
But as time went on, the relationship changed.  Exxon's resources became a double-edged sword.
Former employee Bernard Pueto  later said that the oil giant
gave them too much money and too many directions.
It got Zilog into things they shouldn't have done,
and their young managers didn't have the  experience to know when to push back.
Before long, Faggin was spending more time  over in New York with Exxon trying to keep
them out of the way than he was in California  working with the customers. Disagreements
over Exxon led to Faggin and Ungermann's own  relationship fraying - and the latter exited.
## Taking on IBM
Perhaps the most impactful thing  was that Exxon - unbeknownst to
Zilog - was planning to compete with IBM.
Exxon's tentative first steps into  the office equipment space began in
1975 when it initiated development of  a new typewriter. After several years,
they had themselves the Qyx  "intelligent" typewriter.
Powered by a Z80 chip, this $1,390 typewriter was  billed as the first to be electronic - built with
70% fewer moving parts. The idea was that you  can connect it to the Vydec word processor.
Another product followed - an early version of the  fax machine called the QWIP. It allowed users to
send pages of text or images to others in a few  minutes. Yes, that is what a fax machine does.
These new products apparently gave Exxon  Enterprises confidence and they called
their companies' various senior executives to  come to their New York HQ to brainstorm the
future of IT ... and formulate a grand  strategy to take down IBM and Xerox.
In late 1978, Exxon announced that it had  consolidated the three major products - Vydec,
QWIP, and Qyx - along with 12 other prior Exxon  investments to create Exxon Information Systems.
Exxon wanted EIS - which Sykes said turned $100  million in 1978 and $200 million in revenue in
1979 - to become a big player in the office  equipment space within three to five years.
Some analysts believed that Exxon's  characteristic discipline and focus
can help it win. One at a firm  called Yankee Group said in 1980:
> "It seems likely that the [office system]  business they are building now will rival,
if not surpass, their oil business ultimately"
Yankee Group forecasted that the whole  IT market would be worth $150 to $200
billion by the end of the 1980s and  that Exxon could capture 10% of that.
More than a few were not so positive. Several  cited the size argument again. Exxon pumped $84
billion of revenue in 1979 - fired up by the  high oil prices of the second energy crisis.
Even if EIS got as big as - let's say Xerox,  which sounds like a fantastic feat - that adds
only $7 billion in revenue. For Exxon,  that's a drop of oil into the barrel.
Yet others pointed that smashing  together a bunch of small,
unrelated companies and expecting success is  a fool's errand. Exxon Information Systems
began life with 6,000 employees and  an organization chart 40 pages long.
John Cunningham, EVP at Wang  Labs, colorfully put it:
> "If God himself came down in a junior  businessman's uniform, worked very hard for
three years, and got very lucky, he'd still have  a tough time pulling those companies together"
## Withdrawal
It did not take long for Exxon Information  Systems to start proving Cunningham right.
Exxon had the "luck" of buying into  a suite of old-time word processors
and office products on the eve of  the PC revolution. In April 1977,
Apple introduced the Apple II microcomputer.  Cheap and aesthetically pleasing,
it did wonders when combined with the  powerful Visicalc spreadsheet program.
The growth of digital microcomputers like  the Apple II - including ironically the
TRS-80 computer powered by Zilog's own  Z80 - quickly ate into the antiquated
office equipment market that Exxon was pursuing.
And unfortunately, Exxon had neither  the corporate structure nor culture
to handle a fast moving, talent-centric  environment like information technology.
Faggin recalled just how slowly  the company made decisions, saying:
> So anytime there was a decision to be made, the  lower guy on the totem pole would look up, the
other guy would look up at the next, and Ben Sykes  who was the senior guy would say, “Yes,” or “No.”
The company struggled to develop new products. The  second-generation Qwip machine took six years to
develop and came to the market dead-on-arrival.  Literally. The paper feeder jammed.
There were other product problems.  Vydec was locked out of US government
work due to security issues. A Qyx  intelligent typewriter intelligently
caught on fire inside Exxon’s  own New York City headquarters.
And people at Exxon's marketing division  in Houston explicitly preferred Wang.
They were eventually forced to take Exxon  equipment but returned them a year later.
IBM wasn't exactly the dancing elephant either.  But they had the advantages of a titanic sales
force, cutting edge technology, and the  cultural perception of "nobody got fired
for buying IBM". Even with all that, they still  needed a rebel to go forth and make the IBM PC.
Exxon's status as a competitor by the way  guaranteed that IBM would not choose the Zilog
Z80 to power the PC. Of course, that was not  the only reason behind the decision - it never
is just one - but Faggin later confirmed it did  matter in IBM picking the Intel 8088 over the Z80.
Ben Sykes told the press  that he expected EIS to turn
$400 million in 1980 and keep doubling  to hit a billion within a few years. But
when Exxon increased its investment, its  previously torrid revenue growth stalled.
In 1981, Exxon twice cut its workforce down  from 6,000 employees to just 4,000. They
would shut down some of the QWIP fax machine  factories and reorganize the whole division.
The IBM PC came out that year and changed  the world - further obviating Exxon
Information Systems' already antiquated  lineup. Yet Exxon staggered on for two
more years - its annual report chirping about  losses narrowing and new products coming out.
Then in 1984, the company finally  admitted what everyone else could see:
That this was not working. They started selling  off business lines to whoever was interested.
Everything else was closed down.  According to a former manager,
hundreds of leftover obsolete QWIP machines  were taken to a dump and bulldozed.
## Conclusion
In the end, Zilog was the last company  inside the Exxon Enterprises portfolio to go.
They were sold off in the late 1980s as  a management buyout backed by the private
equity firm Warburg Pincus. The buyout price  was very cheap at about 4 times free cash flow.
Warburg would take it public in 1991  before another acquisition in 1997 for
$527 million - earning the PE firm 12 times  return on a small $17 million investment.
Several of Exxon's other diversification  ventures did better than the office fiasco.
They made good money from developing  residential and commercial real estate
in and around Houston via the  firm Friendswood Development.
They saw more mixed results with minerals  - funding and pursuing various coal, zinc,
molybdenum, and copper mines around the world. And
of course we earlier talked  about the Chemicals business.
But the experience of Exxon Information  Systems imprinted itself deeply upon
Exxon's senior managers. In 1993,  Lee Raymond became Exxon's CEO
and intensified the core message:  They were oil men. Nothing more.
Over the next two decades, he redoubles the  company's efforts in oil and gas. By the late
2000s, ExxonMobil had become the biggest, most  profitable company the world had then ever seen.
